Guide

10 Art Shows to See in Los Angeles This November

Yuntao Xu’s art show in a gas station, LA’s first gallery run for and by Black artists, iris yirei hu’s reliquaries for a dream, and April Bey’s alien tapestries of human life.

The art community in Los Angeles is digging deep into history this November, excavating and reframing it through novel juxtapositions and archival findings. Isabelle Frances McGuire tackles the Salem Witch Trials with a video game that bears uneasy relevance to our current age of creeping authoritarianism (just in time for next week’s midterms). Milano Chow draws on the archives of the LA Public Library to create ghostly architectural facades that seem at once familiar and foreign. At LACMA, an exhibition gives proper due to the city’s pioneering Brockman Gallery of 1967–90, which gave early support to scores of Black artists. And at the Brick, a retrospective brings together the two sides of Todd Gray’s long career: his commercial photos of musical acts and his post-modern tableaux, which themselves pull from archival images to construct new narratives.

Isabelle Frances McGuire: Joy is a Puppet

Bel Ami , 709 North Hill Street, Suite #105 and #103, Chinatown, Los Angeles Through November 28

Isabelle Frances McGuire plays with history, dusting off well-known figures and disrupting their iconic status to enhance their humanity. In Joy is a Puppet , she takes aim at the Salem Witch Trials, a dark period that has taken on increasing relevance as we slide deeper into fascism. The exhibition features a bronze statue, a trio of frogs, an assemblage of baskets, and an interactive video game in which the player takes on the role of a woman accused of witchcraft and must figure out their next move.

April Bey: All the Reasons We Never Tell Someone We Love Them...They’re Worthless

Vielmetter Los Angeles , 1700 South Santa Fe Avenue, #101, Downtown, Los Angeles October 31–December 19

Bahamian-American artist April Bey explores love, romance, and companionship in new fabric works on view at Vielmetter. These pieces represent the latest chapter in Bey’s Atlantica project, in which the artist assumes the identity of an extraterrestrial being and shares dispatches about human life with her home planet. Incorporating crushed velvet, metallic brocade, and sherpa fabric, the large-scale woven tapestries feature portraits that Bey took during a 2024 residency in the historically Black community of Orange Mound in Memphis, Tennessee, depicting scenes of queer intimacy within her opulent textile world.

Charles Arnoldi: String Theory

Michael Kohn Gallery , 1227 North Highland Avenue, Hollywood, Los Angeles Through December 19

Charles Arnoldi has been expanding the terrain of abstraction for almost six decades, from his early twig-and-stick constructions to his chainsaw-carved plywood works and hard-edge geometric paintings. String Theory presents paintings made between 2016 and 2019 in which networks of lyrical lines dance across the surface, their fluid energy contained by the rectilinear boundaries of the canvas. Balancing a sense of visual delight with formal complexity, these paintings are in dialogue with works by Brice Marden, Alexander Calder, and others, while branching out into compelling new directions.

iris yirei hu: Unconscious Relics

Official Welcome , 672 South La Fayette Park Place, Suite 46, Westlake, Los Angeles Through December 19

Iris yirei hu draws on dreams, ancestral knowledge, collective ritual, and elements of the natural world to ground contemporary issues within traditional frameworks. Unconscious Relics features new paintings, ceramics, and reliquary boxes adorned with images and objects that hold personal and cultural significance, originating from Tongva customs and Chinese herbal medicine. Juxtaposing these disparate symbols, hu layers various belief systems in order to create new mythologies for our current, troubled times.

Milano Chow: Fantasy Street and Deborah Turbeville: The Lifted Veil

Hollyhock House , 4800 Hollywood Boulevard, Barnsdall Art Park, Los Angeles Through December 20

Milano Chow creates stark, haunting architectural facades and interiors using graphite, ink, and photo transfer. For the works in Fantasy Street , she ventured into the archives of the Los Angeles Public Library, pulling images of early-20th-century movie theaters, shops, and apartments to construct fictional buildings through ink, pencil, and photo transfer. The works are displayed in an unfurnished room in Frank Lloyd Wright’s Hollyhock House and mounted on folding screens designed by Chow, putting them in conversation with the historic home and blending fiction and reality. Alongside this exhibition, Chow curated The Lifted Veil , featuring surreal, dreamlike photographs by Deborah Turbeville from the 1970s through the 1990s that resonate with her own entrancing alienation.

Yuntao Xu: Estranged Landscape

Adams Square Mini Park Gas Station , 1020 East Palmer Avenue, Glendale, California Through January 8, 2027

Estranged Landscape (2026) (image courtesy Glendale Library, Arts & Culture)

Los Angeles is full of art spaces in unconventional sites — strip malls, storefronts, apartments — and the Adams Square Mini Park Gas Station in Glendale fits right in with that tradition. Within this modest, window-lined box, architect and artist Yuntao Xu has created an installation inspired by the natural landscape surrounding the gas station that houses it. Composed of reflective fabric hung from the ceiling, fluffy textiles, and colored lights, Estranged Landscape echoes the forms of Southern California’s dramatic peaks and valleys with a campy, space-age spin.

Todd Gray: Church and State

The Brick , 518 North Western Avenue, East Hollywood, Los Angeles Through January 16, 2027

Todd Gray’s photographic assemblages mix images of art, architecture, and the natural world in ambitious tableaux that lay bare the intertwining threads of colonialism and culture. Gray got his start as a commercial photographer, however, when he was just a teenager, photographing bands including the Doors, the Rolling Stones, and Led Zeppelin; shooting album covers for Gladys Knight and Bobby Brown; and even becoming Michael Jackson’s personal photographer. Church and State brings together these two bodies of work for the first time, alongside biographical ephemera illustrating Gray’s personal experience as a Black man coming of age in Los Angeles during the 1960s, ’70s and ’80s.

Julie Tolentino: And Never Ends

Fulcrum Arts , 544 North Fair Oaks Avenue, Pasadena, California Through January 23, 2027

And Never Ends (2026) (photo courtesy Fulcrum Arts)

Julie Tolentino’s wide-ranging practice incorporates performance, sound, installation, scent, and text. Fittingly, her current exhibition at Fulcrum Arts aims to “decenter the visual,” encouraging visitors to utilize their other senses, especially hearing. Eschewing a static presentation, this new installation includes cultured crystals, an auditory composition, and a performance-based drawing, creating an environment that will continue to change and develop throughout the exhibition’s run.

The Brockman Gallery: Los Angeles, 1967–1990

Los Angeles County Museum of Art , 5905 Wilshire Boulevard, Mid-Wilshire, Los Angeles Through January 24, 2027

The Brockman Gallery was LA’s first major art gallery founded and run by and for Black artists, exhibiting the work of David Hammons, Ulysses Jenkins, Suzanne Jackson, Senga Nengudi, Betye Saar, and others early in their careers. Founded in 1967 by brothers Alonzo and Dale Brockman Davis shortly after the Watts Rebellion, the gallery served as a vital cultural and community hub in Leimert Park until its closing in 1990. This is the first large-scale exhibition dedicated to the gallery, tracing its history and legacy through over 60 artworks and archival material.

Reggie Burrows Hodges: A Theater of Dreams, A Theater of Miracles, A Theater of Passions

Art + Practice , 3401 West 43rd Place, Leimert Park, Los Angeles California African American Museum , 600 State Drive, Exposition Park, Los Angeles Getty Center , 1200 Getty Center Drive, Brentwood, Los Angeles Through February 28, 2027

This three-venue exhibition showcases the work of Los Angeles-born artist Reggie Burrows Hodges, with expressionistic paintings that highlight his deep engagement with art history intertwined with autobiographical narratives and scenes of contemporary Black life. A Theater of Miracles showcases the influence of Old Master paintings in his work, including several at the Getty, such as Jacopo Bassano’s “The Miracle of the Quails” (1554), which will be on display at CAAM. Meanwhile, A Theater of Passions exhibits new paintings inspired by the work of father-and-daughter painters Orazio and Artemisia Gentileschi in the Getty’s collection. Finally, A Theater of Dreams at Art + Practice reflects on the artist’s childhood growing up in Compton and his travels through Europe, where he encountered many of these Old Master paintings in person.

article_text:
ARTnews , Art in America , and Artforum just wrapped up the inaugural edition of Art Week NYC , a citywide event celebrating all the New York art world’s ecosystem has to offer, from museums and galleries to artists, collectors, and cultural tastemakers from the Lower East Side and Tribeca to Chelsea and the Upper East Side.

Art Week NYC kicked off with an opening party at the Mallory in Chelsea, a 19th-century warehouse building that used to be home to the Tunnel nightclub. Programming took place over four jampacked days, from November 11–14. A launch event at the Metropolitan Museum of Art had in attendance New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, City Council Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams, Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal; New York State Senator Jose Serrano, and City Council member Virginia Maloney. David Breslin, the Met’s curator in charge of the modern and contemporary art department, referred to Art Week NYC as “a defining tradition in our city’s cultural landscape—and that’s saying a lot.”

On November 13 and 14, ARTnews hosted a slate of programming at PMC’s ground-floor studio across the street from the New York Public Library. The two-day event was presented by Amazon, in partnership with Louis Roederer Champagne, Piaget, and Flying Whale Wines.

Friday featured in-depth conversations with art world insiders, such as dealers David Nolan and Anton Svyatsky on what separates collectors from speculators; Tina Vaz, the MTA’s director of arts and design, speaking about several newly announced public art commissions; and photographer Stephen Shore detailing his new book, The Mental Image , a mix of memoir, pictures, and art history. Top 200 Collectors Larry and Allison Berg discussed the increasing crossover between sports and the art world, while art adviser Sophia Cohen gave insights on how a new generation of collectors is reshaping the market.

On Saturday, ARTnews welcomed two of our sponsors to the PMC Studio: Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s Head of Patrimony, talked about Andy Warhol’s love of timepieces and how the watchmaker came to collaborate with the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, while Frédéric Rouzaud, president of Maison Louis Roederer, discussed lasting ways for private patrons, like the Louis Roederer Foundation, to support contemporary art.

The day also looked back on what has happened to art in the 2020s (so far), synthesizing the impact of the pandemic, the NFT boom and bust, the rise of AI, and social and political upheaval; featured a spirited chat with New York Magazine ’s Jerry Saltz on the current state of art criticism and the art world; and explored the importance of art collecting as both a personal passion and a creative practice from the point of view of two fashion executives, Carolina Herrera global creative director Wes Gordon and Oribe cofounder Daniel Kaner.

Before bidding farewell to our very first Art Week NYC, ARTnews revealed the winners of the third annual ARTnews Awards . This year’s jury included top curators from across the United States, and you can read more about the categories and the winners here .

article_text:
Issue

New Currents: Heesoo Kwon

HEESOO KWON ,

Leymusoom Garden: New Sun , 2024, still from 3D animation: 14 min 21 sec. Courtesy the artist.

In Heesoo Kwon’s Leymusoom Sinmok (2023), thin branches gathered from Ohlone land are suspended in midair, bearing fraying, knotted strands of hanbok and sochang fabric, wool crochet, and other inherited textiles. These remnants of female labor are entangled with discarded hardware—LED lights, cables, a computer mouse—together embodying the digital mysticism that characterizes Leymusoom, Kwon’s autobiographical feminist religion-cum-artistic universe and the namesake of her fictional serpentine creator goddess.

Born in Seoul and currently based in the US, Kwon leverages technology and archival materials to create a “metaverse-sanctuary” dedicated to the feminine Other, subverting the patriarchal dynamics encoded in Korean folkloric belief and her own Catholic upbringing.

article_text:
Frida screenwriter and Selena writer/director Gregory Nava is mourning the loss of his friend Dolores Huerta, the civil rights icon who died today at age 96.

Nava and his wife Barbara Martinez Jitner were by Huerta’s side in her final moments.

“We were blessed to be by Dolores’s side last night in Bakersfield, to say goodbye and stand with her family in love. Dolores was a great light and a fearless warrior for justice. She set the world ablaze with her passion for equality and inspired generations to discover their own power,” they said in a joint statement.

Related Stories

Toho CEO Matsuoka Hiro On The Company's Decision To Self-Distribute 'Godzilla Minus One' In The U.S. -- Tokyo

Milwaukee Brewers Win First World Series In Franchise History

Throughout her life, Huerta fought for the rights of many, including, in large part, that of farmworkers and their families. Channeling that passion into action led her to co-found the labor union, the National Farm Workers Association, alongside Cesar Chavez, which later became United Farm Workers. She organized multiple boycotts that forced the agriculture industry to shift, leading to improved working conditions and the passing of legislation that secured the migrant farmworkers’ rights to bargain collectively, among many other achievements.

Watch on Deadline

Finding inspiration in Huerta’s life, Nava announced in 2024 that his next film would be a biopic on Huerta, a passion project he will direct from a screenplay he co-wrote with Martinez Jitner. Earlier today, Nava confirmed the script has been completed, and he and his team will be taking the next steps to move the project along.

For many years, Huerta turned down offers to have her story told on the big screen, but she changed her mind. In recent years, she realized that a movie would be a way to inspire the next generation of activists and organizers.

Nava and Martinez Jitner’s message also said, “In these last few years, Dolores and her beautiful family welcomed us even closer, entrusting us with the telling of her life-its extraordinary courage, its struggles and joys, its deepest pain. It has been one of the greatest privileges of our professional lives, and a deeply personal trust. We will honor it with tenderness and care, carrying her voice and her story to generations yet to come.”

The upcoming film’s producer Ivette Rodriguez remembered spending time with Huerta in the past three years as the legendary activist’s story continued to unfold.

“Dolores inspired generations to recognize their own power and fight for dignity and justice. This is an extraordinary loss, and my heart is with her family. It has been the greatest honor to know Dolores and to work with Gregory and Barbara, whom she entrusted with her life story. That trust is a profound responsibility—one that will be honored with the love, care, and respect she deserves,” Rodriguez said.

Huerta is also admired for being a staunch supporter of women’s and voters’ rights who didn’t shy away from pushing Washington to change policies for the better, even in later years. She is famously known for coining the term “Sí, se puede,” a rallying cry used first during a hunger strike in 1972. The term was translated into English as “Yes, we can,” most famously used by Barack Obama in 2004 during his run for the U.S. Senate and again in 2008 when he ran for president—both times with Huerta’s full support. President Obama awarded Huerta the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012.

Before Nava’s new film hits theaters, Huerta can next be seen participating in the Ellen Gavin-directed Blood Money , a four-minute short film that examines the billion-dollar business behind America’s ICE detention system, the human cost of immigration enforcement, and the power of collective action. The project serves as one of her last on-screen appearances.

article_text:
VENUS ALFA è un viaggio nel sottosopra della cultura visiva tra storie kinky, glitch culturali e cattive ragazze che sfidano gli stereotipi, hackerano il gender gap e amplificano il female empowerment.

In La morte ti fa bella (1992), Robert Zemeckis raccontava l’ossessione per la giovinezza eterna e l’estetizzazione del corpo femminile attraverso una commedia nera diventata cult. L’elisir dell’immortalità, agognato dalle protagoniste Madeline Ashton ( Meryl Streep ) e Helen Sharp ( Goldie Hawn ) e custodito dalla misteriosa Lisle Von Rhoman ( Isabella Rossellini ), finiva per ridurle a veri e propri manichini viventi, condannati a una manutenzione grottesca e disperata, mentre i loro corpi cadevano letteralmente a pezzi. Nel mondo dell’arte contemporanea, invece, il legame tra corpo, tempo che passa e mortalità abbandona i toni della finzione per tradursi in una ricerca espressiva lucida e spietata.

Se nel film la morte si manifesta come il paradossale prezzo da pagare per il tentativo di sfuggirle, nella storia dell’arte il rapporto con la mortalità si è spesso intrecciato alla figura dell’artista, al suo vissuto e alla sua stessa scomparsa. Per lungo tempo l’archetipo dell’artista tormentato, segnato da una vita complessa o da una fine prematura, è stato associato soprattutto a figure maschili, da Caravaggio a Van Gogh , fino a Jean-Michel Basquiat . Quando il trauma, la fragilità o la morte hanno riguardato le donne, lo sguardo esterno ha spesso tentato di ricondurre tutto a una dimensione più romantica o a un fatto di cronaca. Diverse artiste e studiose contemporanee hanno tuttavia proposto una prospettiva diversa, trasformando la vulnerabilità, la memoria e il corpo che si consuma fino a scomparire nella materia prima del proprio lavoro.

Un esempio emblematico è quello di Francesca Woodman , morta suicida a New York nel 1981 a soli ventidue anni. Spesso raccontata attraverso l’etichetta dell’artista maledetta, la sua fotografia rivela in realtà una ricerca delicata e rigorosa sul corpo. Nei suoi scatti in bianco e nero, la figura umana è sfocata, si confonde con le carte da parati che si scrostano o si fonde con gli intonaci di case abbandonate, esplorando con sensibilità il confine tra presenza e assenza.

Se con lei il percorso è poetico e intimo, la storia della critica d’arte Francesca Alinovi mostra un’altra sfaccettatura del rapporto tra vita, morte e racconto. Docente al DAMS e curatrice di grande intuito, Alinovi fu tra le prime a cogliere la potenza della Street Art newyorkese, portando in Italia autori come Keith Haring e Basquiat. Profondamente immersa nella scena punk e dark degli anni ’80, viveva l’avanguardia con un’energia e uno stile unici. Ma quando nel 1983 fu brutalmente assassinata nel suo appartamento di Bologna, l’attenzione morbosa dei media trasformò la sua fine in un caso di cronaca nera, feticizzandone l’immagine e mettendo a lungo in ombra la straordinaria portata del suo contributo intellettuale.

E come non citare la celebre “bad girl” Tracey Emin , da sempre abituata a mettere a nudo le proprie ferite, come nell’iconico My Bed . Oggi Emin sta vivendo una stagione di straordinario successo mondiale e consacrazione istituzionale. Dopo aver rischiato di morire nel 2020 a causa di un tumore aggressivo ed essere sopravvissuta a un devastante intervento salvavita, il sistema dell’arte e i media sembrano quasi volerla elevare a una sorta di martire contemporanea o figura salvifica. Emin, tuttavia, utilizza questo immenso palcoscenico per mostrare senza filtri i segni della malattia e i radicali cambiamenti del corpo, trasformando la consacrazione mediatica in una presenza potente, carne viva e priva di qualsiasi edulcorazione.

Dalla battaglia contro la Mietitrice al contatto diretto con lei, questa è l’inversione che fa invece l’artista messicana Teresa Margolles , portando l’esperienza vis-à-vis in galleria in modo crudo e sconvolgente. Avendo lavorato a lungo negli obitori di Città del Messico, Margolles, celebrata quest’autunno da una monumentale doppia mostra al MoMA e al MoMA PS1 di New York, utilizza nelle sue installazioni materiali reali legati al decesso e alla violenza, dall’acqua usata per lavare i cadaveri alla nebbia vaporizzata derivata da tessuti organici, trasformando la fine fisica in una traccia tangibile, poetica e al contempo spietata.

La morte ti fa bella, si sa, ma prima «Devi prenderti cura di te stessa. Ricordati: quando sei morta, sei morta!» (Helen Sharp, La morte ti fa bella , 1992).

article_text:
Chris Pratt is teasing his return to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) to reprise his role as Star-Lord from Guardians of the Galaxy .

After Guardians Of The Galaxy Vol. 3 , the post-credits assured fans that the “Legendary Star-Lord Will Return,” but that has not happened yet.

With Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars seeing the MCU come together, Pratt’s Star-Lord could potentially return in one of those films. In a new interview, the actor teased that something is in the works.

“I have a great relationship with Kevin [Feige] and Lou [D’Esposito], and there have been both ongoing conversations about how we make good on that promise and also hard action taken to make sure that we make good on that promise,” Pratt said on The Playlist podcast, The Bingeworthy .

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Michael Douglas Asked To Be Killed Off Marvel's 'Ant-Man': "They Wouldn't Let Me"

Mark Ruffalo Really Hasn't Forgiven Gavin Newsom For Backing Paramount-WBD Merger; That Could Be A 2028 Problem For Potential POTUS Contender

Pratt added, “So yeah, you’ll see Star-Lord again, which is very exciting, but I’m not at liberty to say when that’s going to be, but he’s not going anywhere.”

The Parks & Recreation alum first played the role of Peter Quill in 2014’s Guardians of the Galaxy . Pratt would then reprise the role multiple times across the MCU. In 2017, the actor starred in Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2, and in 2018 he reprised his Star-Lord role in Avengers: Infinity War .

Pratt would later reprise his role in 2019’s Avengers: Endgame , 2022’s Thor: Love and Thunder , 2022’s Disney special The Guardians of the Galaxy Holiday Special, and 2023’s Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 .

It was not only on television and in film that Pratt can be seen as Star-Lord, but he also appears daily at theme park attractions like Guardians of the Galaxy: Mission: Breakout! at Disney California Adventure and Guardians of the Galaxy: Cosmic Rewind at Epcot, the theme park at the Walt Disney World Resort in Florida.

title_original: Carroll Dunham Calls His Filthy Formalism “Abstraction with a Hard-On”
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "I thought it best to confess up front that I was still forming an opinion about his work. Carroll Dunham took that like a gentleman. He is familiar, he made clear to me during ourranginginterview, with the two main camps of interpretation about his potty-mouthed paintings and drawings: 1) that he is a high formalist with an ear for the unconscious seldom rivaled since Surrealism, and 2) that he is a simple vulgarian.", "links": [{"text": "Carroll Dunham", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/carroll-dunham/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I’m lucky people even want to write about my work,” Dunham said. “I made the paintings. They can say whatever they want.” At 76, Dunham is thin, likable, and frank. He has a sharp, deadpan face framed by transition lenses and Beckettian white hair. When we spoke in his studio in Connecticut, he wore a silk suit in the shade of gray-green the French call caca d’oie , the shirt buttoned only in the top half, cholo style, with chunky sneakers in the same shade."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The spacious upstairs had been given over to small abstract sculptures he was making out of aluminum sheeting with assistants. It was July, and Dunham was between two capstone surveys of a long career. A show of his drawings spanning 1974 to 2024 had recently come down at the Art Institute of Chicago, while curators at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, were finalizing a survey of his paintings from 1983 to the present for December. It was the kind of summary moment an artist is lucky to be alive for."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/IMG_3586-2.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Carroll Dunham in his home studio in Cornwall, Connecticut. Photo Laurie Simmons", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Since the ’90s, Dunham’s best-known pictures have starred carefully framed cartoon penises, vaginas, and anuses in varying states of specificity, usually attached to the bodies or the faces of humanoids engaged in sex or violence. This scenery belongs to a tradition of ridiculous bodily extremes, from Greek vases to Thomas Rowlandson to Gustave Courbet to Nicole Eisenman. His style, meanwhile, belongs to the black outlines and dropped-in colors of cartoons. That graphic clarity seems to ask us to read his bodily subjects loud and clear, without any of the technical seduction of peers like Lisa Yuskavage or John Currin."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Although his loud and lusty scenarios committed no real transgression (Peter Saul took care of that in the ’60s, then Robert Mapplethorpe in the ’80s), what may genuinely surprise the uninitiated is the academic remove that characterizes the writing about Dunham. His work is discussed—and discussed primarily by those born before 1975—almost exclusively in the specialist language of form or space or paint application, with little reference to the subject matter. It seems that the writers in Camp 1 understand the shock factor that attends men dildoing their rectums with pistols, or angrily ejaculating on each other from enormous penis-noses, as ammunition against the claim that subject should dictate one’s opinion of a painting. As if to deny the charge of prudery, some of them describe moments of rapture. On a Dunham painting made between 2006 and 2012, of a giant woman spreading her anus and vagina above a landscape like a parade float, the artist Paul Chan wrote of feeling transported: “When I entered the room where it hung [at the Whitney], I gasped. The painting was at once exuberant, provocative, and entrancing. It literally took my breath. I quickly glanced at the other people in the room. Was anyone else having an asthma attack looking at this? ”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Representing Camp 2 are John Yau ( The Brooklyn Rail , 2007: “Saul is an iconoclast and Dunham is a wannabe.”) and a young man in a basketball jersey I met at the Chicago show. This man was examining a pencil scribble from 2020 of a fist clasping an erection, the balls parted and meatus shaped like a teardrop. I asked him what he thought, and he said, “I feel like I’m being pranked.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/IMG_3623-2.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dunham walked me to the “other studio,” a smaller room reserved for painting, where acrylic tubes lay neatly on a table in gradients, labels down. A canvas he had just finishedstood on sawhorses. It showed a man with long black hair down on all fours in a sculpture studio. The painting is called Looking for Something , and its protagonist’s pants are on the floor. His skin is white, and a woman, who is purple, kneels behind him, her head thrown back in a wail or moan. With her hand, she does something to the man’s ass that is not visible to us. In the foreground, another purple person, a Peeping Tom, watches them through a window. Nine of these most recent “Sculptor” paintings, from about Covid to now, were to go up at the Matthew Brown gallery in Manhattan in September as a sort of appetizer for the Miami show."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I asked where these recent purple/white folks come from. “They come from my work,” Dunham explained. “And I don’t mean that to be glib. They really do. So to even answer that question, I would have to go, ‘Before I was doing these paintings, I was doing these paintings, then these paintings,’” he continued, miming with his hands successive leaps into the past."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/MB-CD116.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Carroll Dunham: Looking for Something , 2026. Photo Pierre Le Hors/Courtesy Matthew Brown, Los Angeles and New York/ ©Carroll Dunham", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "BORN THE FIFTH IN A line of Carrolls to a Connecticut poultry farmer who turned to real estate, Dunham went to Phillips Academy (Andover), class of 1967. The sculptor Mel Kendrick was his roommate. “Tip was doing Rapidograph drawings,” Kendrick recalled as we spoke by phone, using Dunham’s nickname. “Almost hippie drawings, very fine sketches.” (Of “Tip,” Dunham said, “It’s a WASP thing.”) Kendrick also recalls Dunham’s appetite for science fiction. (Face-down on his studio table, I spotted James L. Cambias’s Darkling Sea. ) Dunham took darkroom classes. In the school’s literary magazine, his finely exposed photograph of a pouting and rotund lady in a playground swing illustrates a poem by Anthony Grafton, the historian-to-be. “Anything he did, he always had a touch,” Kendrick said. “Tip is very specific. And that’s something I don’t know if people know about his paintings, even now.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "After a year at the University of Rochester, Dunham followed Kendrick to Trinity College, in Hartford, where they worked in a small studio art department. “That meant smoking a lot of dope and reading Artforum ,” said Dunham. On weekends, Dunham and Kendrick would drive down from Connecticut in Dad’s (Carroll IV’s) pickup truck, Kendrick recalled, to sample the new galleries in Soho—Bykert, Paula Cooper, Sonnabend, OK Harris—and to feast on spaghetti and jug wine at the apartment of their Trinity teacher Terence LaNoue."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "LaNoue made almost three-dimensional combine paintings with poured latex and molds. He “was a great teacher, but I always had a kind of resistance to what he was making,” Dunham said. “And I’ve been that guy. I know that I’ve had good experiences between students and me where it really didn’t have to do with them being that turned on about my work.” Dunham never followed, either, in the footsteps of the artist with whom LaNoue installed him for a formative internship. Dorothea Rockburne produced—and still does, at 97—large, clean panes of paper or vellum, lined geometrically or coated in graphite. But the two got on, and still do. “Brighter than almost anybody around,” Rockburne said of him by phone."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What attracted Dunham was the planning implied by Rockburne’s planes—she taught him and Kendrick “how to handle a T-square and other basic things,” she said. He was also drawn to the repetitious text paintings of Mel Bochner (who lived with Rockburne), and to the heaps of raw material arranged by Barry Le Va and by Richard Serra. On graduating, he moved into a loft on Thomas Street shared with Kendrick and Peter Wheelwright, the architect. His 1970s and ’80s in New York were “isolation lite,” he told me. Dunham was part of no scene, he said, but befriended the photographers of the so-called Pictures Generation, and married one: Laurie Simmons . For seven years he worked in a frame shop, then for another seven at Time magazine, as a layout artist, all the while plotting his entrance into the art world.", "links": [{"text": "Laurie Simmons", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/laurie-simmons/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/CD-1984-PA-002.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Carroll Dunham: Fourth Pine , 1982–84. Courtesy Matthew Brown, Los Angeles, New York/©Carroll Dunham", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "DUNHAM ’ S ’70s ART BEGAN with single-line squiggles on canvas or paper. Some are elegantly coiled springs, while others resemble long strings dropped to the floor, their loops filled with ground colors of fast-drying casein or acrylic. He debuted with them at Artists Space in 1981, the Chicago survey was their first time on view since. Rockburne sees little of herself in Dunham’s famous later work. “It had that kind of [Sol] LeWittian, instructional aspect,” said the artist John Newman, another Dunham confederate from those days, by phone. “In the ’70s, drawing was sort of raised to a new place,” Newman explained, “as a much more immediate and idea-oriented kind of territory that wasn’t so laden with the history of painting and sculpture.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The string-loops soon became blobs. When Dunham found the lid of a shipping crate on the street, around 1980, and used that for his surface, the almost sculptural grains and knots of the plywood veneer became guidelines for even more specific and conflicting blobs all mashed together—amoebas, geysers, wilting donuts, kinked tubes, beans, ripples, Froot Loops—in palettes ranging from medical textbook to clown paint. It is with these plywood paintings that the Miami survey begins. From 1984 to ’88, they appeared in three shows at the Baskerville + Watson gallery, with the middle show limited to monochromes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“When the veneer things came out,” Newman recalled, it was amazing. “Think about the first time you ever read James Joyce. You really had to step up to it, participate in it. It was new information.” The art dealer David Nolan “hated them” at first, he said by phone: “I thought these garish, psychedelic colors were just there to shock me, and I just wasn’t interested.” But after a while, he began “to peel away the layers and see how they’re put together. And once I understood that, I thought, Oh God.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/CD-1982-PA-001.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Carroll Dunham: Babysitter , 1982. Courtesy Matthew Brown, Los Angeles, New York/©Carroll Dunham", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The third show sold out before even opening, scoring acquisitions by the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney, and the Brooklyn Museum. Dunham quit his magazine job. Gestural painting had been deemed safe again by young galleries, and although Dunham used a brand of biomorphism that didn’t quite fit with the headliners—Basquiat, Baselitz, Schnabel—he was made. Instead of buying up pallets of plywood and sticking safely to what worked, however, Dunham pivoted again. By the ’90s, his veneer paintings migrated to stretched linen, this time as single forms. They began to elongate into screaming fish-lipped mouths, nugget bodies, wincing faces, and undeniable penises. “They weren’t until they were,” Kendrick said of these organs. Nolan noticed them, too. But since they were untitled, Nolan said, “I thought he was avoiding what was right in front of our noses. They are bodily explosions. I asked if he had tried to be provocative with his art, then or now. The exceptions from sex—lumpy tree scenes and landscapes—became the transgression. From there, he went more humanoid. In the past 20 years, his nuggets have grown up, first into suited G-men with fedoras and angular suits, then into cleanly clarified cartoon nudes, their globe buttocks outlined in elegant black and set in plain landscapes or rooms. They wrestle, fight, bathe, masturbate, copulate, and blind each other. They examine their gaping anuses, their big labia like bike tubes, and their nipples like air-hockey pushers."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/CD-2015-PA-004.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Carroll Dunham: Horse and Rider (My X) , 2013–15. Courtesy Matthew Brown, Los Angeles and New York/©Carroll Dunham", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These characters occupy about half the Miami paintings. article_text:
I thought it best to confess up front that I was still forming an opinion about his work. Carroll Dunham took that like a gentleman. He is familiar, he made clear to me during ourranginginterview, with the two main camps of interpretation about his potty-mouthed paintings and drawings: 1) that he is a high formalist with an ear for the unconscious seldom rivaled since Surrealism, and 2) that he is a simple vulgarian.

“I’m lucky people even want to write about my work,” Dunham said. “I made the paintings. They can say whatever they want.” At 76, Dunham is thin, likable, and frank. He has a sharp, deadpan face framed by transition lenses and Beckettian white hair. When we spoke in his studio in Connecticut, he wore a silk suit in the shade of gray-green the French call caca d’oie , the shirt buttoned only in the top half, cholo style, with chunky sneakers in the same shade.

The spacious upstairs had been given over to small abstract sculptures he was making out of aluminum sheeting with assistants. It was July, and Dunham was between two capstone surveys of a long career. A show of his drawings spanning 1974 to 2024 had recently come down at the Art Institute of Chicago, while curators at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, were finalizing a survey of his paintings from 1983 to the present for December. It was the kind of summary moment an artist is lucky to be alive for.

Since the ’90s, Dunham’s best-known pictures have starred carefully framed cartoon penises, vaginas, and anuses in varying states of specificity, usually attached to the bodies or the faces of humanoids engaged in sex or violence. This scenery belongs to a tradition of ridiculous bodily extremes, from Greek vases to Thomas Rowlandson to Gustave Courbet to Nicole Eisenman. His style, meanwhile, belongs to the black outlines and dropped-in colors of cartoons. That graphic clarity seems to ask us to read his bodily subjects loud and clear, without any of the technical seduction of peers like Lisa Yuskavage or John Currin.

Although his loud and lusty scenarios committed no real transgression (Peter Saul took care of that in the ’60s, then Robert Mapplethorpe in the ’80s), what may genuinely surprise the uninitiated is the academic remove that characterizes the writing about Dunham. His work is discussed—and discussed primarily by those born before 1975—almost exclusively in the specialist language of form or space or paint application, with little reference to the subject matter. It seems that the writers in Camp 1 understand the shock factor that attends men dildoing their rectums with pistols, or angrily ejaculating on each other from enormous penis-noses, as ammunition against the claim that subject should dictate one’s opinion of a painting. As if to deny the charge of prudery, some of them describe moments of rapture. On a Dunham painting made between 2006 and 2012, of a giant woman spreading her anus and vagina above a landscape like a parade float, the artist Paul Chan wrote of feeling transported: “When I entered the room where it hung [at the Whitney], I gasped. The painting was at once exuberant, provocative, and entrancing. It literally took my breath. I quickly glanced at the other people in the room. Was anyone else having an asthma attack looking at this? ”

Representing Camp 2 are John Yau ( The Brooklyn Rail , 2007: “Saul is an iconoclast and Dunham is a wannabe.”) and a young man in a basketball jersey I met at the Chicago show. This man was examining a pencil scribble from 2020 of a fist clasping an erection, the balls parted and meatus shaped like a teardrop. I asked him what he thought, and he said, “I feel like I’m being pranked.”

Dunham walked me to the “other studio,” a smaller room reserved for painting, where acrylic tubes lay neatly on a table in gradients, labels down. A canvas he had just finishedstood on sawhorses. It showed a man with long black hair down on all fours in a sculpture studio. The painting is called Looking for Something , and its protagonist’s pants are on the floor. His skin is white, and a woman, who is purple, kneels behind him, her head thrown back in a wail or moan. With her hand, she does something to the man’s ass that is not visible to us. In the foreground, another purple person, a Peeping Tom, watches them through a window. Nine of these most recent “Sculptor” paintings, from about Covid to now, were to go up at the Matthew Brown gallery in Manhattan in September as a sort of appetizer for the Miami show.

I asked where these recent purple/white folks come from. “They come from my work,” Dunham explained. “And I don’t mean that to be glib. They really do. So to even answer that question, I would have to go, ‘Before I was doing these paintings, I was doing these paintings, then these paintings,’” he continued, miming with his hands successive leaps into the past.

BORN THE FIFTH IN A line of Carrolls to a Connecticut poultry farmer who turned to real estate, Dunham went to Phillips Academy (Andover), class of 1967. The sculptor Mel Kendrick was his roommate. “Tip was doing Rapidograph drawings,” Kendrick recalled as we spoke by phone, using Dunham’s nickname. “Almost hippie drawings, very fine sketches.” (Of “Tip,” Dunham said, “It’s a WASP thing.”) Kendrick also recalls Dunham’s appetite for science fiction. (Face-down on his studio table, I spotted James L. Cambias’s Darkling Sea. ) Dunham took darkroom classes. In the school’s literary magazine, his finely exposed photograph of a pouting and rotund lady in a playground swing illustrates a poem by Anthony Grafton, the historian-to-be. “Anything he did, he always had a touch,” Kendrick said. “Tip is very specific. And that’s something I don’t know if people know about his paintings, even now.”

After a year at the University of Rochester, Dunham followed Kendrick to Trinity College, in Hartford, where they worked in a small studio art department. “That meant smoking a lot of dope and reading Artforum ,” said Dunham. On weekends, Dunham and Kendrick would drive down from Connecticut in Dad’s (Carroll IV’s) pickup truck, Kendrick recalled, to sample the new galleries in Soho—Bykert, Paula Cooper, Sonnabend, OK Harris—and to feast on spaghetti and jug wine at the apartment of their Trinity teacher Terence LaNoue.

LaNoue made almost three-dimensional combine paintings with poured latex and molds. He “was a great teacher, but I always had a kind of resistance to what he was making,” Dunham said. “And I’ve been that guy. I know that I’ve had good experiences between students and me where it really didn’t have to do with them being that turned on about my work.” Dunham never followed, either, in the footsteps of the artist with whom LaNoue installed him for a formative internship. Dorothea Rockburne produced—and still does, at 97—large, clean panes of paper or vellum, lined geometrically or coated in graphite. But the two got on, and still do. “Brighter than almost anybody around,” Rockburne said of him by phone.

What attracted Dunham was the planning implied by Rockburne’s planes—she taught him and Kendrick “how to handle a T-square and other basic things,” she said. He was also drawn to the repetitious text paintings of Mel Bochner (who lived with Rockburne), and to the heaps of raw material arranged by Barry Le Va and by Richard Serra. On graduating, he moved into a loft on Thomas Street shared with Kendrick and Peter Wheelwright, the architect. His 1970s and ’80s in New York were “isolation lite,” he told me. Dunham was part of no scene, he said, but befriended the photographers of the so-called Pictures Generation, and married one: Laurie Simmons . For seven years he worked in a frame shop, then for another seven at Time magazine, as a layout artist, all the while plotting his entrance into the art world.

DUNHAM ’ S ’70s ART BEGAN with single-line squiggles on canvas or paper. Some are elegantly coiled springs, while others resemble long strings dropped to the floor, their loops filled with ground colors of fast-drying casein or acrylic. He debuted with them at Artists Space in 1981, the Chicago survey was their first time on view since. Rockburne sees little of herself in Dunham’s famous later work. “It had that kind of [Sol] LeWittian, instructional aspect,” said the artist John Newman, another Dunham confederate from those days, by phone. “In the ’70s, drawing was sort of raised to a new place,” Newman explained, “as a much more immediate and idea-oriented kind of territory that wasn’t so laden with the history of painting and sculpture.”

The string-loops soon became blobs. When Dunham found the lid of a shipping crate on the street, around 1980, and used that for his surface, the almost sculptural grains and knots of the plywood veneer became guidelines for even more specific and conflicting blobs all mashed together—amoebas, geysers, wilting donuts, kinked tubes, beans, ripples, Froot Loops—in palettes ranging from medical textbook to clown paint. It is with these plywood paintings that the Miami survey begins. From 1984 to ’88, they appeared in three shows at the Baskerville + Watson gallery, with the middle show limited to monochromes.

“When the veneer things came out,” Newman recalled, it was amazing. “Think about the first time you ever read James Joyce. You really had to step up to it, participate in it. It was new information.” The art dealer David Nolan “hated them” at first, he said by phone: “I thought these garish, psychedelic colors were just there to shock me, and I just wasn’t interested.” But after a while, he began “to peel away the layers and see how they’re put together. And once I understood that, I thought, Oh God.”

The third show sold out before even opening, scoring acquisitions by the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney, and the Brooklyn Museum. Dunham quit his magazine job. Gestural painting had been deemed safe again by young galleries, and although Dunham used a brand of biomorphism that didn’t quite fit with the headliners—Basquiat, Baselitz, Schnabel—he was made. Instead of buying up pallets of plywood and sticking safely to what worked, however, Dunham pivoted again. By the ’90s, his veneer paintings migrated to stretched linen, this time as single forms. They began to elongate into screaming fish-lipped mouths, nugget bodies, wincing faces, and undeniable penises. “They weren’t until they were,” Kendrick said of these organs. Nolan noticed them, too. But since they were untitled, Nolan said, “I thought he was avoiding what was right in front of our noses. They are bodily explosions. Come on. ”

DUNHAM HAD BEEN PLENTY aware. He described the ’90s work to me as “abstraction with a hard-on.” But he seemed as bewildered as I about its origin. He spoke with plainness about sex and aggression as if he were a social worker, treating his own work as a sort of passive conduit for those realities. This tone did not seem to me like an act. I asked if he had tried to be provocative with his art, then or now. He said no: “It doesn’t interest me very much … The entire enterprise was provocative.” He spoke of Duchamp’s urinal.

Into the new century and his large survey at the New Museum in New York from 2002 to 2003, which was his last show of that scale until this year, his canvases begin to carry entire buildings and shiploads, colonies and planets full of hateful little nugget people with their penises, guns, and hideous gourd breasts. The exceptions from sex—lumpy tree scenes and landscapes—became the transgression. From there, he went more humanoid. In the past 20 years, his nuggets have grown up, first into suited G-men with fedoras and angular suits, then into cleanly clarified cartoon nudes, their globe buttocks outlined in elegant black and set in plain landscapes or rooms. They wrestle, fight, bathe, masturbate, copulate, and blind each other. They examine their gaping anuses, their big labia like bike tubes, and their nipples like air-hockey pushers.

These characters occupy about half the Miami paintings. In one, Horse and Rider (My X) , 2013–15, a woman holds her arms up in a “Why me?” pose on the back of a horse. The lines of her reach continue south into a stand of flowers and a broken tree branch, dividing the canvas into a perfect X, which Dunham has left visible in pencil beneath the paint. At the geometric center is the woman’s anus, as if to say “Look here.” Just beneath, the horse’s anus gapes, too. He turns back at us with a look like “Excuse you .” (No human or humanoid, however, has eyes in a Dunham work.)

Dunham said of this X composition, “I was very excited when I figured out that that would work.” He explained: “It’s two layers of truth. There’s the subject and whatever that requires to be plausibly rendered.” (He counted “breasts, genitalia, asshole, some notion of limbs, and hair.”) “Then the geometry of the canvas has this other kind of truth, and the two things have to become one thing.” And the woman? “I honestly do not remember why I thought it would be interesting to put a woman on a horse in the paintings.” He thought. “It’s nice to have a black dot in the center of a painting. And it’s even nicer when that black dot is a woman’s ass, you know?”

Nolan was the only one I spoke to who saw strategy in Dunham’s turn to hyper-figuration. He saw the artist “dealing with his own demons or faults about the world.” But he described the work as Dunham did, composition-first. “If you try to forget there’s a face in there, the compositions are very strong.” He advised me to view the paintings upside down, pointing out convincing similarities to Aztecan decoration and adding that recently he, Nolan, had refused to sell one—for a lot of money—until the potential buyer flew to New York to see the shapes in person. “That is a problem with the younger generation. They will lose all of the subtleties.”

WHAT DOES THE YOUNGER generation think? The Miami show this winter (and the Chicago catalog forever) will give them the chance to see Dunham’s career as a single entity and to decide if the evolution of blob to aggression to anus stands up to the hindsight of a more literally minded era. In the purple alien characters on view at Matthew Brown this fall, from the series Dunham calls “Studio on Another Planet” (2022–26), one was hard-pressed not to read a narrative about artists at work in a culture that will misunderstand them: a solitary white male surrounded by voyeurs (critics? dealers? posterity?) as he quietly molds his clay on their land, incurring their sinister attentions. In the last of those canvases, Finished (2019–2025), the aliens have had enough. They’ve dragged the artist outside and are now quartering him to death.

“You’re not supposed to get it,” Newman said of Dunham’s pictures. “Art is about having an experience.” Newman speaks, Darwin-like, of Dunham’s characters emerging from the primordial soup of the plywood paintings. “Younger people probably don’t know the early work. And I actually think if they did, it would help them understand his later work better.” In my conversations with Camp 1, I began to wonder if there has ever been a generation more permissive, more game, than the one that had Dunham as a sort of living symbol of egress: out of the hermetic tasks of Minimalism, through pure shape, into a future where human fictions of any extreme can live without excuse or embarrassment. And I began to envy them.

I asked Dunham if he believed pure abstraction existed. He said yes, adding, “And I think that when I started my work, I was doing it. And then I think at a certain point I realized that it fascinated me to try to add some really literal aspects of just being a human being incarnated, or incarcerated, however you think about it, in a body.”

But I didn’t fully buy Dunham’s hermetic account of his own work as “always in some way self-referential.” There seems to be plenty of lived Artist v. World in his pictures and posture, and plenty of visual breadcrumbs leading to the culture at large. I asked, for instance, which cartoons he watched with his two children, who were born in 1986 and ’92. His eyes widened. “ Ren & Stimpy was good,” he said of John Kricfalusi’s unhinged and influential program. “But the masterpiece of ’90s cartooning as far as I’m concerned was Angry Beavers ,” which he watched with his son. I was fishing. The affinities between Dunham’s ’90s work and the prevailing depravities of Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network are inarguable; and in those affinities, a new generation may see homage to the last golden age of a truly transgressive child-absurd.

Speaking of his younger child, Dunham flashed back: “He came into my studio a lot. He would pick up on things I was drawing and then he would draw stuff of his own that was kind of like that. So I got a lot of, you know, 6- and 7-year-old energy coming back at me about my own work.” Dunham smiled. “It definitely encouraged a certain kind of energy. It’s very sweet to think about actually.”
excerpt_original: Ahead of his Miami retrospective, the artist and his allies help a skeptic understand his work.

article_text:
Films and events

Create

The Story of Documentary Film (The 1990s)

This fascinating chapter from Mark Cousins’ epic essay on the history of documentary chronicles a decade of formal reinvention and mainstream success.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Mark Cousins

UK 2026. 120min

Courtesy of Dogwoof

Language English

Introduction

Cousins, the creator of the groundbreaking The Story of Film: A New Generation and Women Make Film, trains his distinctive film-historian lens on the evolution of documentary. The result is a rich tapestry of landmark works and underappreciated gems. In this illuminating chapter, he guides us through the 1990s, a decade of filmmakers exploring bodies, spirituality, labour, war and politics, against the backdrop of rising commercial interest in the form.

Chloé Trayner

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury and nudity.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Act 3

The latest in Christine Molloy and Joe Lawlor’s series of cinematic essays is a rich and thought-provoking journey through ageing, legacy and the intersection between artistic and personal relationships.

Dependence

A filmmaker sifts through decades of home movies to understand her father, in this intimate study of what it means to love an addict.

Mark Cousins: The Story of Documentary Film

Acclaimed filmmaker and writer Mark Cousins joins us for a fascinating exploration of documentary cinema.

editorial_title_zh: Puedes verlo todo (You Can See Everything) – 纪录片影评
editorial_excerpt_zh: 与其说是一部纪录片，《Puedes verlo todo》更像是一部关于操纵以及无法呈现事实客观性的宇宙恐怖片。原文《Puedes verlo todo (You Can See Everything) – Crítica de la película documental》首次发布于Cine…

"Puedes verlo todo (You Can See Everything) – 纪录片影评", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lalo Ortega", "links": [{"text": "Lalo Ortega", "url": "Puedes verlo todo (You Can See Everything) – 纪录片影评", "caption": "", "credit": "Cine PREMIERE", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.cinepremiere.com.mx/uploads/2026/10/banner-skin-inferior-RetoFoto-scaled.gif?t=1795744575", "alt": "Banner Central Desktop", "caption": "", "credit": "Cine PREMIERE", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.cinepremiere.com.mx/uploads/2026/10/banner-skin-movil-RetoFoto.gif?t=1795744575", "alt": "Banner Central Mobile", "caption": "", "credit": "Cine PREMIERE", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "与其说是一部纪录片，《Puedes verlo todo》更像是一部关于操纵以及无法呈现事实客观性的宇宙恐怖片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“摄影即真相，而电影是每秒24格的真相，”这句著名的格言常被归功于让-吕克·戈达尔（Jean-Luc Godard），但实际上是他在1963年的间谍剧情片《小兵》（Le Petit Soldat）中由主角说出的台词。尽管这并非其本意，甚至恰恰相反，但这句话经常被理解为对电影唤起甚至揭示真实而纯粹真相的权力——这种假设的、被浪漫化的权力的表达。当我们走近由兰斯·奥本海姆（Lance Oppenheim）与内森·菲尔德（Nathan Fielder，他同时也是主演）联合执导的纪录片《Puedes verlo todo (You Can See Everything)》时，有必要记住这种讽刺。影片开篇记录了伊丽莎白·霍姆斯（Elizabeth Holmes）在获得自由最后的日子里，这位因其颇具争议的医疗科技公司Theranos涉嫌数百万美元欺诈而被定罪的企业家。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种讽刺也延伸到了奥本海姆、菲尔德和霍姆斯这几个名字的奇特组合上。前者以《某种天堂》（Some Kind of Heaven, 2020）或《文艺复兴集市》（Ren Faire, 2024）等纪录片闻名，其经过计算和策划的视觉风格（有时几乎带有韦斯·安德森式的风格）放大了其拍摄对象固有的人为表演性。后者则以一种游走在真人秀和社交实验边缘的尴尬喜剧风格闻名，在《排练》（The Rehearsal, 2022）和《诅咒》（The Curse, 2023）等作品中模糊了现实与虚构的界限。而后者（即霍姆斯）则是不仅在贪婪的硅谷，乃至整个美国近代史上最具魅力、最引人注目且声名狼藉的诈骗犯之一。这三个人（或者说角色？）对于外观、表演、传达的形象以及魔术般的把戏而言，它们构成了其作品和公众身份的基石。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这就为一部自称是纪录片的影片提出了一个奇怪的困境。电影纪录片自诞生以来，就一直面临着其存在的重大哲学局限性：通过摄像机的中介、个人偏见、人为错误以及其他环境因素来呈现真实、客观真理的（不）可能性。接近一个事实或拍摄对象的“最佳”方式——真实的？符合伦理的？——是什么？是“墙上的苍蝇”那种观察式且近乎苦行的视角更可取吗？还是那种不仅不掩饰其人为痕迹、反而将注意力吸引到自身的真实电影（cinéma verité）的自我意识？戏剧化和情景再现（甚至延伸至虚构，比如基于Theranos事件、由阿曼达·塞弗里德主演的剧集《辍学生》）是接近事实的有效手段吗？对于我们所关心的问题而言，更为重要的是：当纪录片的主题像“真理”或在特定社会政治时刻存在的感受那样虚无缥缈且抽象时，它究竟能做些什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.cinepremiere.com.mx/uploads/2026/11/puedes-verlo-todo-estreno-900x506.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Cine PREMIERE", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "到了这一步，有必要指出对某些人来说甚至在放映开始前就已经显而易见的事：《Puedes verlo todo》并不是一部关于伊丽莎白·霍姆斯及其在向监狱自首前与家人度过最后日子的纪录片，尽管仅仅因为她曾邀请电影制作人到家中进行记录，这似乎正是这位Theranos创始人及其丈夫比利·埃文斯（Billy Evans）的初衷（“你当然可以看到这一切，”她在某个时刻通过短信写给菲尔德以平息他的疑虑）。奥本海姆再次诉诸一种非常具体的风格化手法——使房间和面孔变暗的阴影、视觉上的遮挡、遥远而主观的视点——来暗示实际上我们无法看到一切……即使这种风格上的对位法让我们因认知失调而受到冲击。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大卫·博伦（David Bolen）的摄影充满了电影首支预告片所普及的那种令人窒息的特写镜头。正如菲尔德和霍姆斯之间那次尴尬的交流一样，还有许多类似的交流，这得益于剪辑师（亚当·洛克-诺顿 Adam Locke-Norton）的工作，不仅沉迷于拉长时刻的尴尬，还作为观众让我们面对这样一个事实：即使这一切就在我们眼前，我们也很难认出自己何时正在被欺骗。但今天的日常生活不正是如此吗？从最微小的琐事到最卑劣的种族灭绝，一切都被记录下来，并经过算法过滤，24/7不间断地传输到我们口袋里的屏幕上。", "links": [{"text": "primer avance de la película", "url": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GGJSRFWALTI"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个问题中蕴含着一种安静而持久的不安，奥本海姆及其团队在《Puedes verlo todo》中极好地利用了这一点。纪录片将人们的注意力吸引到这样一个事实上：这里被拯救或呈现的叙事——霍姆斯夫妇试图构建的叙事、大众媒体的叙事、.</", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.cinepremiere.com.mx/uploads/2026/11/puedes-verlo-todo-estreno-pelicula-2026-900x506.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Cine PREMIERE", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但这里有一种着迷而溃烂的恐惧，它隐蔽而又具有存在主义色彩，不仅在于无法在银幕两侧抓取、呈现和认知这种真相，还在于意识到如此多的因素随时可能将其扭曲。也许正是这种恐惧，衍生出了我们在媒体消费中追查争议事件的集体狂热——在这个世界里，我们所有人都是疯狂寻找其玛德琳·埃尔斯特（Madeleine Elster）的斯科蒂·弗格森（Scottie Ferguson），最终却只遇到了朱迪（Judy）。有的人化身AI虚拟形象，有的人出现在由阿曼达·塞弗里德（Amanda Seyfried）主演的剧集中（需要注意的是，阿里·巴卢赞（Ari Balouzian）的配乐在某些时刻极易让人联想起伯纳德·赫尔曼（Bernard Cine

Puedes verlo todo (You Can See Everything) – Crítica de la película documental

Lalo Ortega

Más que un documental, Puedes verlo todo se presenta como un terror cósmico sobre la manipulación y la imposibilidad de representar la objetividad fáctica.

“La fotografía es verdad, y el cine es verdad a 24 fotogramas por segundo”, dice un famoso aforismo atribuido a Jean-Luc Godard, en realidad enunciado por el protagonista en su drama de espionaje El soldadito ( Le Petit Soldat ), de 1963. Aunque no era el punto, sino todo lo contrario, la frase ha sido a menudo entendida como una expresión del poder –presunto y romantizado– del cine para evocar o incluso revelar una verdad auténtica y pura. Una ironía que conviene tener en mente al aproximarnos a Puedes verlo todo ( You Can See Everything ), el documental codirigido por Lance Oppenheim y Nathan Fielder –quien también protagoniza– y que comienza con los últimos días en libertad de Elizabeth Holmes, la emprendedora convicta por fraude multimillonario a través de su polémica compañía de tecnología sanitaria, Theranos.

Ironía que también se extiende a esa particular combinación de nombres, Oppenheim, Fielder y Holmes. El primero, conocido por documentales como Una clase de cielo ( Some Kind of Heaven , 2020) o La feria del renacimiento ( Ren Faire , 2024), cuyo estilo visual calculado y curado, a veces casi en grado wesandersoniano , exalta el artificio performático inherente de sus sujetos. El segundo, famoso por un estilo de comedia cringe que roza con el reality show y el experimento social, desdibujando las fronteras entre realidad y ficción en producciones como El ensayo ( The Rehearsal , 2022) y La maldición ( The Curse , 2023). Y la tercera, una de las estafadoras más carismáticas, notables e infames en la historia reciente no sólo de la avariciosa Silicon Valley, sino de los Estados Unidos. Tres personas (¿personajes?) para quienes la apariencia, el performance , la imagen comunicada, el truco de magia, son la piedra angular tanto de su obra como de sus identidades públicas.

Lo cual presenta un dilema curioso para lo que se presenta como un documental, género cinematográfico que, desde que existe, se ha confrontado con el gran límite filosófico de su ser: la (im)posibilidad de representar una verdad auténtica y objetiva desde la mediación de la cámara, los sesgos personales, el error humano y demás factores del entorno. ¿Cuál es la “mejor” manera –¿auténtica? ¿ética?– de aproximarse a un hecho o sujeto? ¿Es preferible el enfoque observacional y casi ascético de la “mosca en la pared”? ¿O la autoconciencia del cinéma verité que no sólo no oculta su artificio, sino que atrae atención a sí mismo? ¿La dramatización y recreaciones, incluso llevadas a la ficción –como, digamos, en la serie The Dropout con Amanda Seyfried, basada en el caso Theranos– son dispositivos válidos para aproximarse a un hecho? Y más importante para el asunto que nos concierne: ¿qué puede hacer el documental cuando su sujeto es tan intangible y abstracto como “la verdad” o la sensación de existir en un momento sociopolítico determinado?

Llegados a este punto, cabe señalar lo que para algunos será obvio incluso desde antes de iniciar la función: Puedes verlo todo no es un documental sobre Elizabeth Holmes y sus últimos días en familia antes de entregarse a prisión, incluso si, por el puro hecho de haber invitado a cineastas a su hogar para documentarlos, se da a entender que esa era exactamente la pretensión de la fundadora de Theranos y su esposo, Billy Evans (“por supuesto que puedes verlo todo”, le escribe ella por texto a Fielder en cierto momento para calmar sus dudas). Oppenheim recurre de nuevo a una estilización muy específica –sombras que oscurecen habitaciones y rostros, obstrucciones visuales, puntos de vista lejanos y subjetivos– para sugerir que, de hecho, no podemos verlo todo… incluso cuando el contrapunto estilístico nos da choque por disonancia cognoscitiva.

La dirección de fotografía de David Bolen está cargada de esos asfixiantes close-ups popularizados por ese primer avance de la película . Y como ese incómodo intercambio entre Fielder y Holmes, hay varios más facilitados por un trabajo de montaje (de Adam Locke-Norton) que no sólo se deleita en el cringe de prolongar el momento, sino que también nos confronta, como espectadores, con el hecho de que incluso cuando lo tenemos todo a simple vista, es difícil reconocer cuando estamos siendo engañados. ¿Pero no es esa la vida hoy en día, que todo desde la trivialidad más pequeña al genocidio más abyecto son documentados y algorítmicamente filtrados para su transmisión 24/7 a las pantallas en nuestros bolsillos?

Hay una inquietud silenciosa y persistente en esa pregunta, que Oppenheim y compañía capitalizan tan bien en Puedes verlo todo . El documental atrae atención al hecho de que las narrativas rescatadas o representadas aquí –la que intentan construir Holmes y su esposo, la de los medios de comunicación, la de The Dropout y la de la propia película– son, a final de cuentas, constructos moldeados por el trabajo selectivo de la posición de la cámara, la iluminación, el montaje, la música. La verdad objetiva y auténtica es, como ya dijimos, una imposibilidad cinematográfica.

Pero hay un horror obsesivo y purulento, aunque discretamente existencial no sólo en la incapacidad de asir esa verdad, representarla y conocerla en ambos lados de la pantalla, sino en la conciencia de que tantos factores pueden pervertirla en cualquier momento. Quizá de él se desprende nuestra manía colectiva por indagar en hechos polémicos a través del consumo de los medios, en un mundo donde todos somos Scottie Ferguson en busca obsesiva de su Madeleine Elster, sólo para encontrarnos con una Judy. Algunos, en un avatar de IA, otros en una serie con Amanda Seyfried (ojo, no es casual que la banda sonora de Ari Balouzian evoque tanto, por momentos , a Bernard Herrmann). Y la película nos confronta con ello: hay una responsabilidad tanto en lo se crea y se exhibe por entretenimiento al público, como en lo que éste decide consumir con su tiempo y dinero.

Aunque también hay, y debemos decirlo, algunos asuntos espinosos con Puedes verlo todo . El primero es que, en cierto punto, el documental no sólo levanta la duda de si Elizabeth Holmes es una manipuladora o una víctima de manipulación, pues también cuestiona la posible instrumentalización de su imagen, reputación y poder por parte de su esposo. Una pregunta válida, por supuesto, pero demeritada por el hecho de que eso es, en parte, lo que hace la película: utilizar a Holmes cual rubia hitchcockiana, un enigma fetichizado, como centro y emblema de su discurso sobre la imposibilidad de la verdad objetiva en los medios y la manipulación.

Y de ahí se desprende el segundo asunto complejo: que al dirigir nuestra atención hacia la naturaleza de las narrativas como casas de espejos, constructos calculados, Oppenheim y Fielder esgrimen un relativismo fáctico que roza con una conclusión nihilista. Es decir: si todo es fabricado, nada es realmente verdad. Una idea peligrosa en tiempos en que la posverdad algorítmica moldea nuestra realidad política y que, en el caso de Puedes verlo todo , debe ser tomada con pinzas. Independientemente de una posible vulneración ética tanto del proyecto como de sus creadores , sería mejor tomar el ejercicio como una demostración de la importancia del constante pensamiento crítico hacia las narrativas mediáticas, y no como una resignación pasiva a ellas desde la apatía.

Lalo Ortega Este no es el droide que estás buscando. Crítico y periodista de cine, edita el blog de Film Club Café y también publica en La Estatuilla. Anteriormente, fue editor en jefe de Filmelier en México y Brasil, y editor web para EMPIRE en español.

article_text:
Inspiration for a great storyline can come from anywhere — whether that be a classic work of literature or a great pop song.

It’s become somewhat of a bit for “Blue Film” writer-director Elliot Tuttle to reference Lana Del Rey’s music in his screenplays. He’d written three (as yet unproduced) screenplays before his feature debut about a fetish camboy who agrees to spend the night with an anonymous client, who turns out to be tied to his past. Each time, Del Rey released new music while he was working.

Related Stories

Where to Buy Tickets for Broadway's Biggest Shows Through 2027: 'Evita,' 'A Few Good Men,' 'Much Ado About Nothing' and More

“She was always soundtracking what I was doing, so I would include one reference to her in every single thing I was writing,” Tuttle said amid a conversation Variety moderated in partnership with the Santa Fe International Film Festival to salute this year’s 10 Screenwriters to Watch.

For the climax of “Blue Film,” Tuttle borrows a line from Del Rey’s 2023 track “The Grants.” As the older man reflects on the memories he and the sex worker have made of each other, he says, “I’m gonna take mine of you with me.” (Del Rey dropped “There’s a Tunnel Under Ocean Boulevard,” which featured “The Grants,” while he wrote “Blue Film.”)

“It’s so funny because I really did not ever think that anyone would clock that. But then I also made a movie for gay guys, so I should have realized that someone would,” Tuttle quipped, making the theater full of film festival attendees laugh. Recently, he continued, a Del Rey fan account noticed the homage. “It was kind of the coolest I felt during the entirety of putting out this film!”

Tuttle wasn’t the only one influenced by pop music. While adapting John Steinbeck’s “East of Eden” into a Netflix limited series, Zoe Kazan found herself listening to a ton of Olivia Rodrigo, and she kept the Perfume Genius song “Jason” on repeat. “I listened to that probably hundreds of times, and it ruined our Spotify account for the year,” Kazan joked. “It like filled me with a sense of exquisite, precise rage, and that was what I needed for Cathy.”

When Aleshea Harris adapted her award-winning, genre-bending revenge play “Is God Is” for the big screen, she drew inspiration from works by Rihanna and Doechii.

“In my pitch deck for the movie, I had a still from Doechii’s ‘Crazy’ music video,” Harris said. “There’s a lot of unrepentant rage and self-embodiment in that video. And it’s a little weird, which I always thought ‘Is God Is’ is a few clicks left of center.”

Harris continued, “The summer I wrote the bulk of the play, I was listening to ‘Bitch Better Have My Money’ on repeat. … It’s very vivid. The video is so dope. There’s a revenge narrative inside of that video, so the muscle of that is certainly in the spirit of the film.”

When writing “Tony,” the untraditional origin story about Anthony Bourdain’s early years working in Provincetown before becoming the celebrity chef, writing duo Todd Bartels and Lou Howe only used his memoir “Kitchen Confidential” as a jumping-off point.

“My favorite part of the writing process is I see it as an excuse to go somewhere, and so we went to Provincetown … and spent the better part of three days hanging out in the greatest bar in America. It’s called the Colony Tap, which is a place that can only exist in Massachusetts. It’s sort of Celtics and Red Sox and maritime flotsam and jetsam, and sort of the bones of fishermen past,” Bartels said.

There’s something of an “osmosis,” he explained, about letting a location get into your bones like that. “Then when you have to go back to Los Angeles and you’re stuck alone in your cave with Final Draft, it sort of writes itself a little bit.”

When watching the finished film, Howe realized their early life experiences wormed their way into the screenplay, too. “My first job was washing dishes in a fish market on Nantucket. Todd worked in a fancy French restaurant when he was in high school,” Howe said. “There’s something about those experiences with working early in your life — you think you know how to do something, and then you learn the hard way that you really don’t — that feels very universal. That drew us into Bourdain, but it also made it feel so much more universal.

“Mouse” writer and co-director Kelly O’Sullivan summed up the experience of finding inspiration quite simply: “I feel like it can come from anywhere and everywhere.”

Take her film, for example: “Mouse” is a coming-of-age drama about a teen girl and her best friend’s mom who develop a unique bond after tragedy. “My partner and I were referencing ‘Psycho’ a lot, in that one of our lead characters dies very quickly, like 30 minutes in,’” she said. “We were like, ‘How do we get it to feel like this character, who is not our lead character, is Janet Leigh?’ Like we think this is going to be the star and then we subvert it.”

While crafting the film, O’Sullivan said she came to a realization about writing. “For a while, I thought it all had to be highbrow references, and then learning more about writers I love, you don’t have to just be citing poetry; you can be citing a TikTok account if that’s actually inspirational to you.”

“Sense and Sensibility” screenwriter Diana Reid concurred: “I feel like you’re always like swimming in this soup of influences,” she said.

For her adaptation of Jane Austen’s classic, Reid looked to Sally Rooney’s works and referenced another popular rom-com franchise. “There’s a big plot point in the film that’s based on ‘Bridget Jones’ Diary,’ which is kind of funny because it’s like ‘Bridget Jones’ was a modernization of ‘Pride and Prejudice,’ and then I took something from Bridget Jones to put it back in a very traditional adaptation of ‘Sense and Sensibility,’ so it’s like the snake is eating its tail,” Reid shared.

The panel took place the day before the movie, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles, would open in theaters.

“I’m excited and nervous,” Reid said. “It’s such a privilege to work on — obviously — something like Jane Austen, which already has so much cultural capital and a lot of people care deeply about. It’s daunting, but then also it’s a privilege.”

Was anyone else anxious the night before their project debuted?

“The day my show premiered on Netflix, I projectile vomited, so I’d say I was really calm,” Kazan quipped, as the audience cracked up. “It’s great for me,” she added, smiling.

Indeed, things have really worked out for Kazan. “East of Eden” debuted at No. 1 on Netflix’s global chart with 6.5 million views and has spent 3 weeks in the top 10, tallying more than 25.3 million total views. The limited series has ranked in the top 10 in 80 countries and was the No. 1 series in 22 countries this week. (The limited series also drove a 156% global increase in first-time listeners to the audiobook of John Steinbeck’s classic on Spotify.)

“East of Eden” shared top spots on the Netflix charts with Felicia Pride’s series, the revival of the classic comedy “A Different World,” which debuted the week prior.

“I mean, the anxiety — I don’t even have words for it,” Pride said about waiting for her show to launch. “But I also felt like, ‘Thank God it’s finally going to come out.’ Like there was also a relief. You’ve been working so long … you just want it to come out after a while so that you know how people are going to respond and you can get over that part of the process.”

Pride needn’t have worried either. “A Different World” climbed to No. 1 in the U.S. (and at least 14 other countries), and has spent 3 weeks in Netflix’s global top 10, with more than 11.2 million total views. The HBCU-set series was swiftly picked up for Season 2; Pride took a break from writers room to fly into New Mexico to collect her trophy alongside the class of 2026, which also includes Beth de Araújo (writer-director of “Josephine”); Chuko Esiri (screenwriter and co-director of “Clarissa”); and Rebekah Taussig (screenwriter of “Being Heumann”), all honored in absentia.

Curious, Kazan asked how the experience prepping Season 2 differed from the first go-round.

“I just know what the show is now. I don’t feel the pressure of a season two,” Pride replied, sharing her sense of relief and newfound confidence. “I was very clear talking to my execs at Netflix, like ‘I’m just going to do the same thing.’ And there was support [for that], like, ‘Yes, let’s not reinvent this in season two,’ because sometimes shows try to do that, and I don’t think that is a great thing to do.”

Indeed, every writer has their own process — whether that means diving deep into the source material for an adaptation (Pride rewatching every episode of 1987’s “A Different World” while crafting the pilot) or finding deeper meaning in supplemental research (Kazan combing through Steinbeck’s journals); if it means holing up solo (like Harris did writing “Is God Is”) or trading pages with a collaborator (à la Bartels and Howe).

Watch the full video above as the panel unpacks their methods for getting their brilliant ideas onto the page, then the screen.
